Pele Yoetz 197:5: 4. Hatred, vengeance and grudge-bearing are grave sins, constantly transgressing several positive and negative commandments, and they drag along the hated strife, for “hatred stirs up strife” (Proverbs 6:12), and many evils and troubles follow after it. But one who overlooks his own honor — they overlook all his transgressions for him (Yoma 23a).
Pele Yoetz 197:6: 5. Envy, lust and honor drive a person out of the world (Avot 4:21). Therefore be very, very humble of spirit, for “the hope of man is [but] a worm” (ibid.). “Man is like a breath” (Psalms 144:4). What are we and what is our life; and “a man does not so much as bruise his finger below unless it is decreed from above” (Chullin 7b). If the Lord told him to curse, what is his crime — he acted in accordance with what seemed right to him; and why should a living man complain, [let him rather] overcome his sins.
Pele Yoetz 197:7: 6. One who gains honor through his fellow's disgrace, and one who humiliates his fellow publicly, has no share in the World to Come (Bava Metzia 59a). All these are branches and offshoots of pride. Examine this and you will find that it has been the mother of several grave prohibitions.
Pele Yoetz 197:8: 7. Four groups do not receive the presence of the Divine Presence (Sotah 42a): the group of liars, who are considered like idol-worshippers, as it is written (Psalms 101:7), “He who speaks lies shall not be established before my eyes,” and “lying lips are an abomination to the Lord” (Proverbs 12:22); the group of flatterers, who are loathsome before the Lord; the group of scoffers, whose beginning is suffering and whose end is destruction; the group of slanderers, whom King David, peace be upon him, already cut off, as it is written (Psalms 12:4), “May the Lord cut off all flattering lips,” etc.; and whoever is not careful and vigilant stumbles into all of these or some of them.
Pele Yoetz 197:9: 8. Sadness is evil in the eyes of its Master. What place is there for sadness over the vanities of this world? Everything is vanity and vexation of spirit, and whatever the Merciful One does, He does for the good, and why should a living man complain, except over his own sins and whatever they have caused — and even this specifically at a time of sadness, such as when saying confession or the order of Tikkun Chatzot [midnight lament] and the like; but at a time of joy, that is, when serving the Lord and fulfilling His commandments, “Israel shall rejoice in its Maker” with great joy, as it is written (Deuteronomy 28:47), “Because you did not serve the Lord your God with joy and gladness of heart, out of the abundance of all things,” etc. Therefore let Israel say (Psalms 119:162), “I rejoice at Your word,” and “better for me is one hour of Torah and good deeds than all the life of the World to Come,” and there is a time for every desire; let him not exchange it or trade it away.
Pele Yoetz 197:10: 9. Robbery has many branches, and the inclination's deceptions concerning it are many. This is the rule: whoever profits and is helped by falsehood and fraud — this is robbery; and whoever takes something from his fellow without his true goodwill, with a whole heart and a willing soul, [and he only agreed] out of embarrassment, pressure and the like, there is a trace of robbery in it, and there is no difference between robbing a gentile and robbing a Jew — and robbing a gentile adds the grave sin of desecrating God's Name. And whoever robs his fellow of even the value of a perutah, it is as though he took his life and the life of his children (Bava Kamma 119a). And there is no atonement for him until he returns the stolen item or appeases the one he robbed. And as long as the stolen item is in his possession, his prayer is not heard (Ta'anit 16a). “He amasses riches unjustly; in the midst of his days it will forsake him” (Jeremiah 17:11). And he must come back in a transmigration [gilgul] to repay it. And there is no difference between much and little, for God will bring everything into judgment.
Pele Yoetz 197:11: 10. Excessive eating destroys both soul and flesh, for every weekday meal beyond what is needed for one's health goes to the Sitra Achra [the Other Side], and woe to him, for his limbs become impure, since the Sitra Achra has come to dwell upon them, and he has thereby prepared weapons for the evil inclination to wage war against him, until it brings him down to the depths of Sheol. And this applies all the more, a fortiori, to those who make optional weekday feasts and banquets — do they not know that the Sitra Achra takes the leading share among the guests and finds an opportunity to cause them to sin and to cling to them, besides causing severe bodily illnesses, for no creature comes to suffering except through excessive eating and drinking, and he transgresses “do not destroy” regarding the money, body and soul, for money, body and soul are what he is damaging. And one who has understanding will not follow vanity.
Pele Yoetz 197:12: 11. Forbidden foods. One who is not careful stumbles greatly in the grave prohibition of insects, transgressing four negative commandments for every insect [eaten]. And they are commonly found in leaven, fruits and vegetables, and likewise gnats are commonly found falling into food, and there are many other such prohibitions dependent on eating and drinking; and those who are not careful — “their impurity is proclaimed, they cry, unclean” (Lamentations 4:15), and they will not attain the paths of life, for his body has grown up on forbidden food, and he himself becomes literally a “piece of prohibition.” Therefore be careful, be on guard, and flee a hundred gates of the permitted so as not to enter even one gate of the forbidden, and “put a knife to your throat if you are a man of appetite” (Proverbs 23:2).
Pele Yoetz 197:13: 12. One who benefits [from this world] without a blessing is as though he robbed the exalted and uplifted King, and as though he committed sacrilege against the holy things of Heaven (Berachot 35a). And a soul that transmigrates into food or into the holy sparks, he wounds it, and his soul remains dry and empty, for the body is sustained from the food, but the soul is sustained from the blessing. And there are those who imagine that they are reciting the blessing, yet they skip over the mention of the Name and over the roots of the words and letters, in such a way that his blessing is worse than not blessing at all, for he desecrates the Name of the Lord and the word of the Lord thereby, and he still ends up having benefited without a proper blessing. Whoever is a God-fearing man of true feeling should clothe himself in dread when coming to benefit and to bless the Lord, the exalted and uplifted King, for all the good He has bestowed upon him, and he should be careful and take heed to recite his blessings letter by letter, word by word.
Pele Yoetz 197:14: 13. Indeed they said (Abarbanel on Avot 2:13; Midrash Shmuel 2:15), “Prayer without intention is like a body without a soul.” Woe to us, for we have become very impoverished, and we do not know how to focus with the intentions that should be focused on, and we cannot even focus on the simplest of matters, whether from lack of knowledge or because we are as it were digging ourselves out from the distractions of the times, and also our sins withhold the good from us, and a person has no control over his spirit, and a beneficial thought is fleeting as though escaping. At least let us be strong and strengthen ourselves for the sake of our God, and do what is in our power to pray from the prayer book slowly, letter by letter, word by word, and strive to focus even intermittently, back and forth as much as we can; perhaps God will take pity on us and help us, and He, being merciful, will atone for us.
Pele Yoetz 197:15: 14. The congregational responses — “Amen,” “yehei shmei rabba,” “Barechu,” and “Kedushah” — are matters that stand at the summit of the world, and the essential thing in them is intention. In any case, every kind of response, if one says the words in full, produces fruit even for one who does not know how to focus, and he gains great spiritual profit like one who finds abundant spoil. On the other hand, whoever does not strive to respond loses much good, and his punishment is great.
Pele Yoetz 197:16: 15. One who does not focus his intention on the first verse of the Shema when saying “the Lord is One” — that the Holy One, blessed be He, is one, unique and singular, King in heaven and on earth and in the four directions of the world — has not fulfilled the commandment of reciting the Shema. Woe to the unlearned people who do not go to the wise to hear and learn, for their wickedness is great in the land and they have consumed their portion, but whoever walks with the wise grows wise (Proverbs 13:20).
Pele Yoetz 197:17: 16. Our sages, of blessed memory, said (Berachot 8a) that one who has a synagogue in his city and does not enter there to pray is called “a bad neighbor” and causes exile for himself and his children. How much effort must a person exert so as not to acquire this bad name, “a bad neighbor of the Holy One, blessed be He,” and so as not to cause himself or his children to be wanderers, driven to and fro — God forbid — punished with exile, for displacement is hard.
Pele Yoetz 197:18: 17. A man who prays with the congregation is assured that his prayer is favorable and accepted as it is, without its being scrutinized. And even if he is a wicked man, despised and loathsome, “behold, God is mighty and does not despise” [such a one when he joins with the community], and moreover, joining [the congregation] carries with it several included and accompanying commandments, each one worth a great deal. Not so one who prays alone — he loses much good, and his prayer is not accepted before the One who dwells on high, unless he himself is complete and his prayer is complete. Who would dare set his heart on praying alone except in a place of complete necessity? He harms himself, “walking in darkness with no light for him.” And the prayer of the many is always considered greater, for the performance of a commandment by the many is not comparable to its performance by an individual (Torat Kohanim and Rashi, Bechukotai 26:8).
Pele Yoetz 197:19: 18. Let him take to heart, while in the synagogue, that he stands in the palace of the King of Glory, before the exalted and uplifted King, awesome and terrible, and let dread and fear fall upon him, and he should not let his voice be heard upon entering the sanctuary except in Torah and prayer. And whoever speaks mundane words there — his wickedness is great, and especially on Shabbat, it is an additional transgression; therefore silence is best. And even outside the synagogue, speaking in the middle of prayer and the repetition [of the Amidah] is a grave sin, distressing to the soul. And the man who fears the Rock of his sanctity guards his mouth and tongue, guarding his soul from distress (Proverbs 21:23).
Pele Yoetz 197:20: 19. We have learned: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said, every day a heavenly voice goes forth from Mount Horeb and proclaims, saying, “Woe to mankind for the disgrace of the Torah” (Avot 6:2), for whoever does not engage in Torah is called “rebuked” (meaning, as it were, excommunicated). And we have learned: two who sit together without words of Torah between them — this is a session of scoffers (ibid. 3:2). And the sin of neglecting Torah study is as severe as idolatry, illicit relations, and bloodshed (Yerushalmi Chagigah, end of ch. 1). And our sages, of blessed memory, said (Tanna DeVei Eliyahu Zuta 21) that all the troubles that have come and continue to come upon the world are entirely due to the sin of neglecting Torah study, and just as Torah study outweighs all else, so the sin of neglecting it outweighs all else. And it is written (Job 7:19), “You will not let me alone even to swallow my spittle.” Our sages, of blessed memory, explained that on the Day of Judgment they demand an account even for the brief time it takes to swallow saliva, as to what he spent it on, for he must spend all his days in Torah and the service of God or in something that facilitates his service, and nothing more. And it is written (Joshua 1:8), “This book of the Torah shall not depart from your mouth, and you shall meditate on it day and night.” And they said (Menachot 99b), “Go and examine whether there is any hour that belongs neither to the day nor to the night” — [if there is not,] then engage yourself with idle matters, you toil for nothing and give birth to confusion. Happy is he whose labor is in Torah, which was the mother of all life, teaching man good statutes and commandments, which a man shall do and live by them. Whoever desires life, let him cling to the Torah, for it gives life and corrects a person with good counsel, to be complete in his opinions and every good trait, lacking nothing therein. Happy is the man who does this, and the son of man who holds fast to it.
Pele Yoetz 197:21: 20. Just as speech in Torah is [the source] of all good and all perfection, so too, on the other hand, “whoever multiplies words brings about sin,” and whoever sits in the gathering places of the unlearned, who set fixed times for idle talk, has already put his feet in fetters, and the evil inclination has spread a net for his feet. And each one, upon rising from that gathering, has a basket of creeping-thing sins and transgressions hung behind him, such as slander, mockery, lies, vulgar speech, deceptive words, public embarrassment of others, taking God's name in vain, and many other evils. And even if not even one of all these is present, but only idle talk about the country, about the nations and the kingdoms, his wickedness is still great, for our sages, of blessed memory, said that idle words in the covenant of the tongue are like a wasted seed in the covenant of circumcision. And it is written (Malachi 2:17), “You have wearied the Lord with your words.” The Holy One, blessed be He, said: in creating the world I had no weariness before Me; through what am I wearied? Through one who speaks idle words before Me (Shemot Rabbah 13:1). Woe to one born of woman who causes weariness to the exalted and uplifted King. And our sages, of blessed memory, said (Ketubot 5b), “A man should not let idle words reach his ears, for they are the first to be burned among his limbs.” Thus, happy is the man who does not sit in the session of scoffers, but rather sits at the feet of Torah scholars, or dwells alone and is not counted among the unlearned company.
Pele Yoetz 197:22: 21. An evil thought defiles the soul and drags evil after it. Transgression leads to transgression, until he comes to deliberately induced emission and the grave impurity of seminal discharge. And our sages, of blessed memory, already said (Yoma 29a) that improper thoughts of sin are harder than the sin itself. And they said (Niddah 13b) that one who deliberately induces his own emission should be under a ban. And this is not the only case of improper thoughts of sin; greater than this, we have learned (Avot 3:4) that one who turns his heart to idleness [without Torah or worthwhile pursuit] endangers his own soul. And our sages, of blessed memory, said regarding the verse (Leviticus 19:4), “Do not turn to the idols [elilim]” — do not turn away from your own understanding [al da'atchem] (Shabbat 149a). And it is written (Deuteronomy 8:11), “Guard yourself lest you forget the Lord.” Therefore, let a man be firm in strengthening himself to banish alien thoughts and evil musings from his heart, and let him place within himself a light — the light of Torah, and the fear and love of the honored and awesome Lord — and immediately upon remembering that he is not doing good, let him flee and be saved from the mire of the deep, and not look at wrongdoing, and let him correct his crookedness; as it will neither be exchanged nor traded, evil for good. Behold, how good it is, for the commandments to fear and to love are constant commandments, and “they shall be for lights.”
Pele Yoetz 197:23: 22. Looking at women is itself a transgression and drags sin after it, for the eye sees and the heart devises thoughts of iniquity. And it is written (Numbers 15:39), “And you shall not stray after your heart and after your eyes, after which you go astray.” And our holy sages, of blessed memory, have already testified that whoever gazes at women eventually comes to transgression (Nedarim 20a), for it could happen that his children from his own wife become mamzerim, since he is drinking from this cup while setting his eyes on another cup; and evil will also cling to him and he will come to a seminal emission. And even if he merely entertains some improper thought, he will surely be punished for arousing the evil inclination within her and blemishing the eyes of his own soul and the supernal eyes. And this is the judgment of those who “have eyes but see not” in matters of understanding, for their eyes are sealed from seeing, and their hearts from understanding. And our sages, of blessed memory, said (Yerushalmi Berachot 1:5) that whoever does not gaze at women — the Holy One, blessed be He, says, “This is My judgment” [i.e., is on My side]. Therefore let a man be firm in strengthening himself to shut his eyes from seeing evil, and let him not turn to the idols — neither the daughters of Israel nor the daughters of the uncircumcised — and let Israel say, “I have made a covenant with my eyes; how then could I gaze upon a maiden?” (Job 31:1). And thereby no misfortune, plague or illness will befall him, and he will merit to behold the pleasantness of the Lord eye to eye, and he will be a fruitful bough by a fountain [whose eyes overcame the evil eye].
Pele Yoetz 197:24: 23. Intoxicating drink is exceedingly evil, for all the affairs of the world, whether mundane matters or matters of Heaven, require knowledge, for “by knowledge the rooms are filled” (Proverbs 24:4), and every prudent man acts with knowledge, and wages war with strategy against his inclination in order to serve his Creator and cling to Him, and one who reflects on a matter will find which is the straight path a person should choose in order to do what is good and upright in the eyes of God and man. And the sage already said (Vayikra Rabbah 1:6; Tanchuma, Vayikra 1:2), “If you have acquired knowledge, what do you lack? And if you lack knowledge, what have you acquired?” And the truth is that because of our sins we have become very impoverished, and we do not have so much wisdom and understanding to know which is the straight path in which we should walk, and what deeds we should do. If we should still drink and confuse our minds further, what are we and what is our life — this resembles one who deliberately destroys himself. And even without intoxication one does improper things, in excess and in deficiency. And the evil of drinking and drunkenness is that it is a covering over the eyes for everyone, and it is known that whoever errs through it becomes ignorant of knowledge. And those who straighten their ways and wish to have their deeds corrected withdraw their hands from it.
Pele Yoetz 197:25: 24. How exceedingly hated is strife — evil in the eyes of the Lord — and it drags after it many evils, troubles and grave transgressions. Against this, great is peace, especially peace in the home between a man and his wife, to the point that it was permitted to erase the Name written in holiness in order to bring about peace between a man and his wife. And a man is not to be praised merely because his wife and all who accompany him do his will as he pleases and he is at peace with them; rather, one may truly boast when the members of his household or other people stir up strife against him and provoke him to his face and belittle his honor and the like, and he, being a lover of peace, a seeker of peace and pursuer of peace, distances strife and pushes it away with both hands — this man is beloved above and cherished below; happy is he in this world and it is well with him in the World to Come; according to his deed shall his reward be paid; how good is his portion and how pleasant his lot.
Pele Yoetz 197:26: 25. Distance yourself from ugliness and from what resembles it, and do not give room for suspicion of yourself, so that guilt not come to be attributed to you through it, for one who causes another to sin is worse than one who kills him (Bamidbar Rabbah 21:4; Tanchuma, Pinchas 3), and it is written (Numbers 32:22), “And you shall be clear before the Lord and before Israel.” And let him find favor and good understanding in the eyes of God and man, all according to the person, the place, the time and the matter, for regarding something he is compelled to do in order to fulfill his duty to Heaven, he should not worry about the mockery of the complacent, and should not take to heart what others say about him, for this is the root from which stem many injuries and wounds to the soul; and most of the troubles that come upon a person are because he wants to be honored in the eyes of others, and this is a great vanity, for what does it give a man if a thousand people honor him, or if they speak ill of him and disgrace him — will his flesh feel pain because of it? Let the living take this to heart: if he is honored in Heaven above, what does it matter to him regarding the imagined honor of man, which is like a breath; and if he is despised and loathsome in Heaven above, what does the honor of confused spirits give him or add to him — all is vanity and vexation of spirit.
Pele Yoetz 197:27: 26. How very careful one must be not to cause his fellow pain, neither by speech nor by deed, neither by look nor by hint, and he should not do or say anything about which there is even a one-in-a-thousand concern that it could cause pain to his fellow, for our sages, of blessed memory, said regarding the verse (Ecclesiastes 12:14), “For God will bring every hidden thing into judgment” — this refers even to one who spits or kills a louse in front of his fellow, causing him disgust (Chagigah 5a). If this is so — that one who did not even intend to cause pain must one day give an accounting — how much more so one who intends to. And if you say, “As he has done to me, so I will do to him; I will repay the doer of evil according to his evil,” you thereby transgress what the Torah said (Leviticus 19:18), “You shall not take vengeance nor bear a grudge.” And if he is wicked and guilt has come about through his hand, as Scripture says (I Samuel 24:14), “From the wicked comes forth wickedness” — why should his fellow make himself wicked like him? And if you say, “I am merely joking,” you are then making a joke with your own blood and soul, like a madman shooting firebrands. Therefore be careful and take heed that the spirit of humankind be at ease with you, and “love your fellow as yourself” with abundant affection — this is a great principle of the Torah.
Pele Yoetz 197:28: 27. One must be especially careful not to cause pain to one's wife even by words, since her tears come easily, and the punishment for her pain is near. Go and learn from the story brought in the Talmud (Ketubot 62b) about that pious man who was accustomed to come home every eve of Yom Kippur; once he was late in coming, and his wife became distressed and shed tears, and that pious man immediately passed away. Let a man tremble and take hold of himself: if this happened to one who did not even intend to cause pain, how much more so to one who intends to. And even if she is a difficult woman lacking understanding, provoking him to his face and increasing household expenses and the like, wisdom should come from the husband, and he should guide her gently, with pleasant speech, for “a soft tongue breaks a bone” (Proverbs 25:15), and in any case he should bear with great patience, for great is the peace of the home, and he should honor his wife for the honor of the Divine Presence, for these are ancient matters. One who does this in this world will find rest, and “the Lord will command the blessing to be with him” (Psalms 133:3), and his reward is with him and his recompense before him for the World to Come; he shall stand in a horn of light, for the reward is according to the pain (Avot, end of ch. 5).
Pele Yoetz 197:29: 28. Let the great power of counsel be magnified — [the counsel] whose eyes are open upon all the ways of men, to give to a man according to his ways, and “the eyes of the Lord range through all the earth,” and “the whole earth is full of His glory,” for it is within a man's power to be firm in strengthening himself to hear, to teach and to be taught, to keep and to do everything that is a commandment from the Torah or from the Rabbis, or a good custom or a custom of piety, and to flee from every hint of prohibition and from evil traits. Let him be exceedingly fearful of transgressing his Maker's will and angering and paining Him, God forbid, and let him flee from ugliness and from what resembles it even more than he would flee from a sword, for the wrath brought on by sins is a sword, “a sword to the Lord filled with blood,” a sword taking vengeance for the covenant; and “better is one hour of tranquility of spirit in the World to Come than all the life of this world” (Avot 4:17). And if the enemy — the evil inclination — prevailed and led him to transgress his Maker's will, and he committed transgressions and nullified commandments, and habit turned into evil nature and evil traits and evil customs — if he merits that Heaven has mercy on him and his eyes are opened and he recognizes that it is evil and bitter to forsake the Lord, let him hasten to find escape for himself before his calamity suddenly comes upon him, when he will gnash his teeth and be consumed, and his remorse will not help. Therefore, while the sun has not yet darkened, let him correct his crookedness and let the wicked man forsake his evil way; let it be exchanged, let it be traded — little by little he shall drive out the impurity, and wage war with strategies, so as not to anger further the exalted and uplifted King, the One who dwells on high, and he shall atone for the sin against his soul and for the abundant guilt as much as he is able. Whatever is in his power to do, let him do, and whatever a man desires to do, he can do — only the beginning is hard, and thereby he shall find favor, and the Lord will be a refuge for him, and he shall behold the vision of the Almighty; and for one who has a good heart, this suffices.
Pele Yoetz 197:30: These two sets of generalities, the first and the second, I wrote during the days of Shovavim. May it be [God's] will that this be for me a correction as a sign of the holy covenant, Amen; so may it be [His] will.
Pele Yoetz 198:1: Kelalut (Generalities) — Part 2 — I shall write this as a reminder, in brief, of the commandments practiced nowadays that are within every person's power to fulfill every day, and it is fitting for a person to keep them as a reminder before his eyes, and let it surely be recalled aloud. And so it is written in Sefer Chareidim, page 3, column 2 (from which I gather this brief and forceful order of commandments), that it is fitting for every God-fearing person to begin each day by recalling in his heart and uttering aloud all the commandments that can be fulfilled, in order to fulfill the verse (Numbers 15:39), “And you shall remember all the commandments of the Lord and do them” — remembrance leads to action (Menachot 43b), and thereby the Lord will command His kindness toward him, as it is written (Psalms 103:17), “And the kindness of the Lord is from everlasting to everlasting upon those who fear Him, and His righteousness to children's children, to those who keep His covenant and remember His precepts to do them.”
Pele Yoetz 198:2: [1] On three things the (small) world stands: love, fear, and submission. And your mnemonic is: “Ayeh” [“Where”] — the place of His glory, to revere Him.
Pele Yoetz 198:3: [2] There are six constant commandments, which should not cease from a person even for a single moment all his days, and these are they:
Pele Yoetz 198:4: 1. To believe and to reflect upon the existence of the Lord, His individual providence, and the strength of His power.
Pele Yoetz 198:5: 2. To believe that He is One, unique and singular, and there is none besides Him.
Pele Yoetz 198:6: 3. To love Him with a fierce love, with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.
Pele Yoetz 198:7: 4. To fear Him with a great fear, because He is great and rules, the root and source of all worlds, and everything stands as nothing before Him.
Pele Yoetz 198:10: And there are four constant negative commandments:
Pele Yoetz 198:11: 1. That it should not enter one's mind that there is a god besides the blessed Name.
Pele Yoetz 198:12: 2. Guard yourself lest you forget the Lord.
Pele Yoetz 198:13: 3. And you shall not stray after your heart and after your eyes.
Pele Yoetz 198:14: 4. That he not be haughty and his heart not be lifted up; rather, his heart should always be humble like a hyssop.
